metadata.methods_description: Participants sat in a sound-isolating booth and heard stimuli through ER-2 insert earphones at about 60 dB SPL. Phase one presented ten one-minute click trials. Phase two presented 33 shuffled trials each of original and chimeric monophonic music, with 0.5 s pauses between trials. EEG was recorded in BrainVision format. Stimuli were controlled with a Python script using expyfun. Participants also completed a musicianship questionnaire.

citation_details.title: Hierarchical Neural Representations and Divergence Mechanisms in Music and Speech Processing
citation_details.author: Amelia Duarte, Amelia Lindholm, Julian Thorne
citation_details.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH & SOCIAL SCIENCES
citation_details.abstract: The human auditory system possesses an extraordinary capacity to parse complex acoustic environments, extracting meaningful communicative and affective signals from overlapping sensory streams. Among the most intricate of these signals are music and speech, two distinctly human faculties that share fundamental acoustic properties such as pitch, rhythm, and timbre, yet serve divergent communicative and emotional functions. This paper investigates the hierarchical neural representations and divergence mechanisms underlying the processing of music and speech. By synthesizing current perspectives in cognitive neuroscience, auditory processing, and neuroimaging, we elucidate how the brain utilizes shared neural substrates at the peripheral and early cortical stages before deploying specialized, divergent pathways in higher-order association areas. citation_details.title: Chimeric Music Reveals an Interaction of Pitch and Time in Electrophysiological Signatures of Music Encoding
citation_details.author: Shan Tong, Edmund C. Lalor, Ross K. Maddox
citation_details.abstract: Pitch and time are the essential dimensions defining musical melody. Recent electrophysiological studies have explored the neural encoding of musical pitch and time by leveraging probabilistic models of their sequences, but few have studied how the features might interact. This study examines these interactions by introducing “chimeric music,” which pairs two distinct melodies and exchanges their pitch contours and note onset times to create two new melodies, distorting musical pattern while maintaining the marginal statistics of the original pieces’ pitch and temporal sequences. Through this manipulation, we aimed to dissect the music processing and the interaction between pitch and time. Employing the temporal response function framework, we analyzed the neural encoding of melodic expectation and musical downbeats in participants with varying levels of musical training. Our findings from 27 participants of either sex revealed differences in the encoding of melodic expectation between original and chimeric stimuli in both dimensions, with a significant impact of musical experience. This suggests that decoupling the pitch and temporal structure affects expectation processing. In our analysis of downbeat encoding, we found an enhanced neural response when participants heard a note that aligned with the downbeat during music listening. In chimeric music, responses to downbeats were larger when the note was also a downbeat in the original music that provided the pitch sequence, indicating an effect of pitch structure on beat perception. This study advances our understanding of the neural underpinnings of music, emphasizing the significance of pitch–time interaction in the neural encoding of music.

citation_details.title: An updated herpetofaunal species inventory of Iona National Park in southwestern Angola
citation_details.author: Javier Lobón‐Rovira, Pedro Vaz Pinto, François S. Becker, Krystal A. Tolley, John G. Measey, Bruce Bennet, Bastiaan Boon, Sango dos Anjos Carlos de Sá, Werner Conradie
citation_details.abstract: Angola has experienced an incredible increase of the knowledge of its herpetofauna over the past decade. However, accurate biodiversity inventories remain deficient for certain regions of particular conservation interest. We therefore provide an updated checklist of Iona National Park’s herpetofauna, with 75 recorded species, including five amphibians and 70 reptiles, 40 of these recorded for the first time in Iona National Park. These species comprise ~80% of the reptile diversity of Namibe Province. Therefore, this work recognises Iona National Park as the most reptile-diverse protected area in Angola and is potentially one of the richest in southern Africa. Consequently, this work enhances the importance of specific conservation plans in the area and the need for further investigation into the hidden biodiversity of this region.
